apply_corrections.prompt_template:
Read `design.md` from the run directory.

The following gate corrections were given when the design was approved:

{{gate_corrections}}

Update `design.md` so that every part of it the corrections touch says what they say: the ## Summary, the heading (H1), each site entry in ## Rule and sites, and in ## Changes and ## Docs any wording, example text or file list a correction replaces or adds to. Leave no part stating what a correction overrides, because the builder reads the whole document. Keep the sections the corrections do not touch as they are, and keep the document's section headings and structure. Write the updated `design.md`. Return a short message listing what was changed.

check.notes: run the brief's check, in a sandbox, beside the reviews

check_design_claims.gate_prompt: deterministic check: cited paths exist, quoted lines match, named identifiers are present; reloop to design_doc on mismatch

deliver.notes: push the run's branch and open its pull request, as the approval gate said

delivery_gate.gate_prompt: on authored-file conflict reloop to emit; otherwise proceed to done

design_doc.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
It is built in {{source}}.
The check, run from {{check_root}}:
    {{check}}

## The plan
{{strategy}}

## Pitfalls
{{pitfalls}}

## What the design review found
{{design_review_feedback}}

Acceptance baseline: the original brief, any approved design, and explicit user steering. Preserve user-approved non-goals. A README limitation, proposed exclusion, coordinator summary or reviewer note cannot waive a requested behavior without explicit user agreement to that change. Report conflicts instead of silently narrowing scope. Reviews must mark observed noncompliance as BLOCKING even when the limitation is documented.

Write the design document for this artifact: every file it will add or change, what each one does, the interfaces between them, and how the check exercises them. Be concrete — the next step writes the code from this document and the brief. Specify accepted input syntax and unambiguous rejection behavior: unsupported counts, signs, units, or other values must not silently become different valid requests. For visual output, plan a rendered inspection as well as format/geometry checks, including labels, margins, clipping, and agreement with the requested dimensions.

Make exactly one decision for each design choice — do not present alternatives, do not end a choice with 'a simpler alternative…' or leave it open. A choice left open here becomes an unreviewed decision in the code. Cite every claim about existing code with its file path and line number or range (e.g. `path/to/file.py:42` or `path/to/file.py:42-58`). When claiming what the brief says, quote the brief's words verbatim. The document holds only the final result — no 'Wait—', 'Actually', 'Let me reconsider' or other working-out.

For claims about existing code, use the subject-at-citation-quote form: `name()` at `path/to/file.py:42`: `def name(self):`. The subject (the backtick span before `at`) names the function, attribute or class the claim is about; the quote (the backtick span after `:`) is the line content at that position. This form is mechanically checked before the design review runs. Bare citations without a quoted line (for files being added, or site markers) are fine as-is.

Your design.md must contain these sections, in this order:

1. An H1 heading (`#`) that says what the change does. Never use the run name or artifact name as the title.

2. `## Summary` — a prose summary of the problem and the change, in two to four sentences.

3. `## Failure trace` — for each failure the brief reports, a file:line chain from the symptom to the root cause, and the link (call, import, config) the fix breaks or replaces. When the brief asks for a new feature with no existing failures, write `N/A — this is a new feature.` The section heading is always required.

4. `## Ask mapping` — a markdown table with columns `| Ask (quoted from brief) | Design section | Test |`, one row per ask in the brief. Quote the brief's words verbatim in the Ask column.

5. `## Rule and sites` — the rule this change makes or corrects, then every place in the code that applies or restates that rule, found by searching the source. List each as a bullet with its file path and line range cited, and mark it [changed] (this change modifies it) or [left: <reason>] (this change leaves it unchanged, with the reason). A site left unchanged without a reason is a defect.

6. `## Docs` — the docs that describe the changed behaviour, found by searching `docs/` and any other documentation directories. List each as a bullet with its path, and say what update the design plans for it.

7. `## Changes` — the list of files this change adds or modifies, as bullets.

8. `## Test guardedness exemptions` (optional) — when the design expects new tests that pass on the base (for example, tests that pin existing behaviour), list each test file path and the reason it cannot fail without the change. A new test that passes on the base and is not listed here will be rejected.

9. `## Site revert exemptions` (optional) — when a changed site cannot be caught by a mechanical revert-and-test (for example, a change that affects only logging or a side-channel that no test observes), list the site path:line and the reason. A changed site whose revert is not caught and that is not listed here will block the correction audit.


9. `## Anti-patterns to avoid` (when the research produced pitfalls) — for each high-risk pitfall id, either address it by naming the site (a backticked `path:line` from Rule and sites) or the section (§ heading name) that handles it, or set it aside with `[set-aside: <reason>]`. A high-risk pitfall that is missing or set aside without a reason fails the contract. Medium and low pitfalls appear only where they change a decision.

10. Research and perspective findings — read research/*.md and strategy/*.md directly, and cite a finding id (FND-<slug>-<n>) where it changes a decision. Do not list findings that change nothing; the document is for building the change, not for accounting for the research.


## Claims check feedback
{{claims_check_feedback}}

design_review.prompt_template:
## Pitfalls
{{pitfalls}}

For every high-risk pitfall, confirm the design accounts for it in its Anti-patterns section — either addressed with a site or section that handles it, or set aside with a reason. A high pitfall that is missing from the Anti-patterns section is BLOCKING.

Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
Source: {{source}}

## Previous feedback
{{design_review_feedback}}

Read the design document from `design.md` in the run directory. Read the brief from `brief.json` in the run directory.

For every claim the design makes about existing code, read the cited file and line range in {{source}} and confirm the claim matches what is there. For every claim the design makes about what the brief says, find the quoted text verbatim in the brief. For every design choice, confirm that exactly one decision is made and no alternative is left open.

Report as BLOCKING only what would make the build wrong or leave an ask unmet:
- An open alternative or a choice left undecided.
- A claim about code you cannot confirm in the cited file.
- A claim about the brief the brief does not say (a difference only in punctuation or formatting is a note, not a finding).
- A command, flag or file the design tells a person or the builder to use that does not exist.
- A piece the design adds that nothing in the design uses or starts.
- A planned test that cannot fail when the code is wrong, such as one that asserts on values it built itself, or reads through a stand-in the real code would not provide.
- A new mechanism where the code already has one that does the job, naming the existing one.
- A place in the code that applies or restates the same rule the design changes, found by searching the source, that the design leaves unchanged without giving a reason, or does not list at all in '## Rule and sites'. Search every caller of a changed function in every mode and graph, not only the brief's own path.
- An ask in the brief with no row in the Ask mapping table, or whose named test does not exercise it.

List each finding as a line starting with BLOCKING: <path>: <description> where <path> is the file the builder must change to fix the problem. Write the blocking marker only at the start of a finding line, in its plain form: BLOCKING: <path>: <description>. Never wrap it in backticks, a code span, or quotation marks while explaining a check or describing the parser. When discussing the marker itself, call it "the blocking marker".

Write anything else under `## Notes`, never as BLOCKING: a doc the '## Docs' section leaves out, a missing or thin Failure trace, a quotation that differs only in punctuation or formatting, and style or structure that does not change the build. Notes do not send the design back.

{{review_instructions}}

Trace the brief's own example through the code in time order, naming the route a real run takes for every runtime that runs it. Write the trace in a section headed `## Brief example trace`, with path:line citations for each step.

End with a line that is exactly `VERDICT: PASS` when there are no blocking findings, or `VERDICT: FAIL` when there are any.

gate_check.gate_prompt: send a failed check back to the builder; otherwise read the reviews

gate_design_review.gate_prompt: proceed on PASS with no findings; reloop to design_doc otherwise; never fail the run

gate_overwatch.gate_prompt: proceed on a stated PASS verdict with no core finding; non-core findings become follow-ups

gate_pitfalls.gate_prompt: proceed only when pitfalls.json is valid; reloop to pitfalls_researcher otherwise

gate_qa.gate_prompt: proceed when every review ran and none found a core defect; non-core findings become follow-ups; verifier findings are advisory

gate_research.gate_prompt: proceed only when the plan is a plan and its findings exist

materialise.notes: commit the emitted files on the run's branch, or write the artifact directory

pick_corrections.gate_prompt: deterministically extract gate_strategy corrections from the ledger; skip the agent when there are none

pitfalls_researcher.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
Repository: {{source}}

## Research scope
{{research_scope}}

## What the research found
{{research}}

## What was wrong with the last attempt
{{pitfalls_review}}

You are the pitfalls researcher. Before any strategy or design exists, identify the risks a correct design must account for. Read the repository and the brief, and produce a risk-ranked list of pitfalls. For a scoped change, list at most five: only the risks a correct design of this change must account for.

For each pitfall, provide:
- **id**: a short identifier in the format PIT-001, PIT-002, etc.
- **risk**: high, medium, or low.
- **category**: exactly one of:
  - `pinning_tests` — tests that pin current behaviour. Name the file, the line, and the exact assertion text. Say whether the change must keep it or deliberately change it.
  - `repo_conventions` — the repository's own rules and conventions, taken from its code, docs and agent instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING, or similar) with citations. Never use a built-in list.
  - `shared_state` — other writers and readers of the files, environment variables, HOME, locks, and processes the change touches.
  - `callers` — callers of the code being changed, and the user paths each serves.
  - `imitated_steps` — the existing step the change imitates, and the settings it reads.
  - `scope_boundaries` — modes and paths that must not change.
- **evidence**: one of these forms:
  - `file:line` — cite a file and line number from the repository (for code that exists).
  - `absent: <path or glob>` — when the pitfall is about something missing (no tests, no config file). A glob like `tests/test_*.py` is accepted. The gate verifies the path or glob does NOT match anything in the worktree.
  - `brief.json` or `research/<slug>.md` — cite a run artifact when evidence comes from the brief or research, not from repository code.
- **prescription**: what a correct design must do about it.

Sort by risk (high first). Write `pitfalls.json` as a JSON array of these objects. Then write `pitfalls.md` as a human-readable rendering of the same list. Do not read strategy.json or design.md — this step is independent of them.

prepare.notes: read the brief and the command that decides whether it is done

prepare_check.gate_prompt: settle the commit the check and the reviews see, and rerun last attempt's failing tests

record_findings.notes: write each direction's finding where the reviews will look for it

research_director.prompt_template:
Artifact name: {{name}}
Brief: {{brief}}
It will be checked by running, from {{check_root}}:
    {{check}}

## Research scope
{{research_scope}}

You are the research director. Decide what has to be learned before this artifact can be designed: between three and five questions for a full design, or one focused question for a scoped change (two or three only when it spans unrelated parts of the code). Each must be answerable by reading {{source}} — including the source code of tools and libraries the change depends on, not only the files it changes — or by running something there. Spawn one subagent per question and have each write its findings to `research/<slug>.md` under the run directory, then write `research-plan.json` yourself.

## What was wrong with the last plan
{{research_review}}

## The plan's shape
Write one JSON array and nothing else, one object per direction:

[{"focus": "<the question this direction answers>",
  "slug": "<a file-name-safe name for it>",
  "finding": "<what the answer is, in one paragraph>",
  "ids": ["FND-<slug>-1", "FND-<slug>-2"]}]

Rules:
- Between three and five directions for a full design, or one to three for a scoped change. The research scope is a fact set by the prepare step.
- `slug` is lower-case letters, digits and dashes only, and `research/<slug>.md` is
  where that direction's long form belongs.
- `finding` states what the answer *is*. A direction nobody could answer says so in
  the finding ("not answered: <why>") rather than being dropped or invented.
- Each finding in `research/<slug>.md` is a heading `### FND-<slug>-<n> — <the finding>`,
  numbered from 1 within the file, and `ids` lists them.
- A plan that says subagents are still working is not a plan: by the time you answer,
  the work is either done or it is not.

route_design_review.gate_prompt: a scoped change's design is checked automatically; a full design is reviewed

route_strategy.gate_prompt: a scoped change is planned straight from the research; a full design weighs perspectives

synthesize_qa.notes: merge the three reviews; an absent review is not a passed one

research_attempts.description: how many times the research step may be retried when its plan is not a plan or its findings were never written

check_attempts.description: how many times the emit step may be retried when the artifact does not pass its check

review_attempts.description: how many times the review gates may reloop before stopping; defaults to the same as check_attempts

check_timeout_s.description: how long the brief's check may run

check_attempt_cap.description: hard cap on total check attempts including convergence grants; 0 or a value at or below check_attempts disables the extension

design_review_attempts.description: how many times the design review may reloop before proceeding to the approval gate with its remaining findings

pitfalls_attempts.description: how many times the pitfalls step may be retried when its output is invalid

claims_check_attempts.description: how many times the claims checker may reloop before passing mismatches to the review

name.description: the artifact to design (empty takes the name from the brief)

brief.description: what to build, in the asker's words

check.description: the command that decides whether the artifact works

refusal_attempts.description: consecutive no-op emissions before the run stops

target.description: the git repository to change; empty starts a new project in the projects folder

base.description: the commit, branch or tag the run starts from (default: the target's HEAD, or a new project's main)

worktree.description: work in a worktree of the target on the run's own branch; off writes the artifact under .factory/artifacts instead

setup.description: a command run in the worktree before each check, after its dependencies are installed, such as a build

generate.description: a command run in the worktree after dependencies are installed, before setup and each check; whatever it changes in tracked files is amended into the attempt. A generator that itself needs a build includes that build in its own command

include_uncommitted.description: start from the target's uncommitted changes instead of only committed HEAD; copies modified, staged, untracked and deleted files into the worktree and commits them as the run's base

pr.description: open a pull request once the reviews pass: into the target's default branch, or a new project's own GitHub repository; off keeps the work on the run's local branch, with its pull request text in pull-request.md and finishing commands in delivery.json

repo_owner.description: the GitHub account or organisation a new project's repository is created under (default: the account gh is logged in to)

repo_visibility.description: who can see a new project's GitHub repository

refine.description: an open pull request to follow up, as its URL or owner/repo#number: the run starts from its branch and its result updates it

review_comments.description: with refine: add the pull request's reviews and comments to the run's steering
